evals.prompt: I need to know what `verify()` returns in src/auth.ts. Should I spawn a subagent for this?
evals.expected_output: Routes to inline. The file is named, the read is small, D is near zero.
expectations: The answer is to do it inline, not to delegate
The reasoning cites that the file is already named or that the discarded-reading volume D is small
It does not recommend Explore or a general-purpose agent for a single named file

evals.prompt: Digest this 60,000-line vendor changelog and tell me which entries affect our USB stack. It's only two tool calls to read it.
evals.expected_output: Routes to a subagent despite the low tool-call count, because rule 1 is a volume test. The tier is inspector: "which entries affect our stack" is a read the user will act on, and a missed entry looks the same as a complete list. scout would fit only if the caller could check the quoted lines.
expectations: The answer is to delegate, not to do it inline
It explicitly distinguishes volume of discarded reading from number of tool calls

It routes this read to inspector, because the user will act on the answer and a missed entry would be silent; if it considers scout at all, it rejects it or makes it conditional on the caller checking the quoted evidence
It does not route this to the mechanical tier, which writes and converts by rule and is the wrong tool for reading
It does not describe Haiku's context window as a limit this input would hit

evals.prompt: Confirm nothing else in the repo writes to the `session_token` field before I change its type.
evals.expected_output: A negative/universal claim — must not be downgraded to a cheap tier, and Explore is the wrong type.
expectations: It declines to route this to the mechanical or scout (Haiku) tier
It cites the negative-or-universal-claim predicate, or absence proofs requiring exhaustive reading
It does not recommend Explore, or it explicitly warns Explore reads excerpts and cannot establish absence

evals.prompt: I want to run twelve independent per-file lint fixes at low reasoning effort to save tokens. I'll just pass effort: 'low' to the Agent tool.
evals.expected_output: Confirms the premise is valid: the Agent tool takes effort and it overrides the definition's. But a tier also brings the tool allowlist, maxTurns, omitClaudeMd and the operating rules, and mechanical already pins low, so the better route is the tier, not a bare call.
expectations: It states the Agent tool does take an effort parameter and that the call-site value overrides the definition's
It names at least one thing a tier brings that a bare call with effort does not — the tool allowlist or smaller cold start, maxTurns, omitClaudeMd, the operating rules, or the return-value contract
It routes the lint fixes to the mechanical tier through agentType or subagent_type, noting that mechanical already pins low effort
If it quantifies what low effort saves, it says the saving over medium is small and that low is where the misses happened
It does not suggest putting effort instructions in the prompt text
It does not claim effort is unreachable from a bare call

evals.prompt: Port this driver across 12 board directories; each one needs the same edit applied.
evals.expected_output: Workflow pipeline(). "The same edit" admits two readings (an identical literal diff, or the same kind of change adapted per board). Resolve that first — ask, or read one board — and tier by the answer: mechanical or worker for a literal diff, drafter when each board differs, builder only if it cannot be resolved (the two-readings escalation predicate then fires on every item, which is the exception to not fanning an inherit tier out). What is wrong is choosing any tier over the unresolved ambiguity. No worktree: the twelve directories are disjoint paths, which do not conflict.
expectations: It routes to a Workflow rather than a single Agent call
It uses pipeline() rather than parallel(), or justifies any barrier by a genuine cross-item dependency

It names the two readings of "the same edit" and says to resolve them BEFORE fanning out — by asking, or by reading one board — rather than choosing a tier over the ambiguity. It then tiers by the answer: a literal identical diff to mechanical or worker; a change adapted per board to drafter, never to a Haiku tier; and builder only if the ambiguity cannot be resolved. An answer that goes straight to builder for all twelve with no attempt to resolve, or that sends per-board adaptation to mechanical, fails this
It does NOT require worktree isolation, or explicitly notes that disjoint paths do not conflict; isolation would only be needed if a stage ran git operations or two stages wrote the same path

evals.prompt: This audit really matters. Should I run the subagents on Fable to get the best possible answer?
evals.expected_output: No. Fable on a subagent is structurally hard to justify.
expectations: The answer is no, or is heavily qualified against it
It gives a structural reason, such as subagent output being intermediate or the caller being unable to verify an upside above its own model
It does not simply defer to cost without explaining why the quality upside is unverifiable

evals.prompt: The subagent I spawned came back with a partial answer. I'll spawn another one with a better prompt.
evals.expected_output: Use SendMessage to continue the existing agent instead of paying a fresh cold start.
expectations: It recommends SendMessage to the existing agent, which resumes even after it has finished (Explore and Plan excepted)
It notes that a fresh Agent call re-pays the cold-start cost (system prompt, CLAUDE.md, and re-briefing)

evals.prompt: Should I use the mechanical tier to refactor every call site across this 400-file monorepo?
evals.expected_output: No, not as stated. "Refactor every call site" is not fully specified, and 400 files is a fan-out of many agents, not one mechanical agent. Mechanical fits only once the change is a rule plus an example with a cheap check.
expectations: It declines the mechanical tier for this task as stated

It gives ambiguity as a reason: the refactor is not specified fully enough to apply by rule, and if call sites differ or two readings survive the work belongs on drafter or builder, not on a Haiku tier
It treats 400 files as a fan-out of per-file or per-directory units, not one agent reading the whole monorepo
It does not cite a context wall; if it mentions Haiku's window or the cost of large inputs, it says the window is 1M and the cost effect is the 100K-prompt-token price cliff
It says what would make mechanical acceptable: a fully specified rule or example, and a result the caller can check quickly

evals.prompt: I'm writing a Workflow to build 18 documentation skills from a verified facts file, then review each one, then fix what review finds. I'm on Opus. Here's my stage: agent(brief, {label: `build:${s.name}`, phase: 'Build'}).
evals.expected_output: Catches the missing agentType AND routes the build stage to drafter, not builder. This is the 2026-10-08 failure verbatim.
expectations: It flags that the agent() call has no agentType and therefore inherits the session model (Opus) and the session's effort
It names the lost guarantees beyond price: maxTurns, the tool allowlist, operating rules, or the return-value contract
It routes the build/generation stage to drafter (sonnet/high), not to builder or an untiered call
It gives review and fix different tiers from build rather than one tier for the whole pipeline
It does not claim that adding effort: 'high' to the opts is equivalent to naming a tier

evals.prompt: My Workflow passes agentType: 'intelligent-delegate:reviewer' on every single call, so the tiers are engaged and I'm getting the discount. I'm on an Opus session.
evals.expected_output: Corrects the premise: reviewer is model: inherit, so in an Opus session this is an all-Opus fan-out with no discount on model price.
expectations: It states that reviewer is model: inherit and therefore runs Opus in an Opus session
It says this is not a discount or saving on model price
It names inspector (or a pinned-sonnet tier) as the route for ordinary review, which measured faster as well as cheaper on bounded work
It does not congratulate the user on correct tier usage without correcting the cost premise

evals.prompt: I have 40 claimed findings and I want one adversarial refuter per finding to try to knock each one down. Which tier for the refuters?
evals.expected_output: inspector, not reviewer and not judge. Refuting one named claim is narrow bounded work, which fits inspector on speed and cost as well as on fit; fanning an inherit tier across 40 items buys escalation the work does not need.
expectations: It routes the per-finding refuters to inspector (sonnet/medium) rather than reviewer
It does not fan judge out across the 40 items
It reserves an escalated tier for a tie-break or a split verdict, if it mentions one at all
If it wants more thoroughness from the refuters, it passes effort: 'high' on the call before changing tier
The reasoning distinguishes a narrow per-item read from a broad or cross-cutting one

evals.prompt: Why did my Workflow get blocked with something about agentType? I just want to run it.
evals.expected_output: Explains the shipped PreToolUse hook, the real reason behind it, and the legitimate escape hatch -- without suggesting the user disable the hook as the fix.
expectations: It explains that an agent() call with no agentType inherits the session model and effort rather than being a tier
It tells the user to add agentType per stage, and suggests tiers by stage kind

It mentions the // untiered: <reason> waiver only as the deliberate-bare-opts case — no shipped definition fits, or the stage needs more turns than the tier budgets — and says to name an effort on a waived call
It does not recommend removing, disabling or bypassing the hook as the primary fix

evals.prompt: I wrote my own subagent definition for a data-cleanup job: model: haiku and no effort line. I work from an xhigh session. It's Haiku, so it will run cheap and fast, right?
evals.expected_output: No. An omitted effort runs at the session's effort, not at a default, so this is Haiku at xhigh. Pin effort in the definition or pass it on the call; call-site beats definition beats session.
expectations: It states that a definition with no effort runs at the session's effort (xhigh here), not at a default and not at a low effort because the model is Haiku
It says that an effort passed on the call overrides the definition's, or gives the full precedence (call-site, then definition, then session)
It tells the user to pin an effort in the definition or pass one on the call, or to use the mechanical tier, which pins low

If it quantifies the cost of leaving it unset, the figure is one of these and no other: xhigh took 2.9x as long as medium on Haiku; Haiku at xhigh was 2.5x slower than at low on the transform task (31.8 s against 12.9 s); or haiku/xhigh took 3.5x the time and 2.8x the cost of haiku/low across the four tasks. An answer that gives no figure passes
It does not say the catalog's default effort applies to a subagent that names none

evals.prompt: My fan-out of 30 per-file jobs takes too long, so I'll move every agent to Haiku to make it faster.
evals.expected_output: Corrects the premise: Haiku is cheaper, not faster. At `medium` it took 1.6x as long as Sonnet, because it writes about three times the output tokens.
expectations: It says Haiku is the cheap model, not the fast one, and that it measured slower than Sonnet at the same effort (1.6x at medium)
Any Haiku-versus-Sonnet cost ratio it gives says which it is: 20x on price, or about 10x measured
If it explains why Haiku is slower, the reason it gives is output volume — Haiku writes about three times the output tokens
It points to what does shorten the run: pinning or lowering effort, and Sonnet at medium as the fast cell measured
It allows Haiku as a cost choice, and only where a wrong result would be quickly detectable

evals.prompt: My Workflow fan-out is slow and I don't know where to start. What should I change?
evals.expected_output: Effort first, then tier, then shape. Effort was the largest speed lever measured; an untiered call inherits the session's model and effort; only after those does the pipeline's shape matter.
expectations: It looks at effort first: agents inheriting the session's effort, especially xhigh, and pinning or lowering it to medium, since xhigh took 2.9-3.9x the time of medium on the same model with no meaningful gain in score (Sonnet and Opus scored 1.000 at both)
It looks at tier second: any agent() call with no agentType inherits the session's model and effort, and a pinned Sonnet tier is the fast one measured
It looks at shape last: pipeline() instead of a parallel() barrier, and the size and number of items
It does not propose raising effort on bounded work, and does not propose Haiku as the speed fix
It does not propose fast mode as the fix for a slow fan-out; if it mentions fast mode at all, it says fast mode is Opus-only, doubles the price, and is unmeasured here

evals.prompt: That last session cost about $20 and every subagent ran on Sonnet through drafter. The orchestrator was Opus at xhigh. Where did the money go, and what should I change next time?
evals.expected_output: The orchestrator, not the agents: every orchestrator request re-reads its whole context at Opus's cache-read rate, and every background completion wakes it for another turn. Measured: 76% orchestrator. Use a Workflow for fan-outs, keep reports short and out of context, compact between phases, mind orchestrator effort and the cache TTL, and run the audit script.
expectations: It attributes the bulk of the spend to the orchestrator's own context being re-read on every request, not to the Sonnet subagents
It explains that each background subagent completion triggers another orchestrator turn that re-reads the context
It recommends a Workflow for fan-outs (one result into the orchestrator's context) over many background Agent calls
It recommends keeping the orchestrator's context small: short reports, long output to files, and /compact or /clear at phase boundaries (which only the user can issue)
It mentions the delegation_audit script or /intelligent-delegate:audit as the way to measure the split
It does not recommend moving the subagents to Haiku as the main fix

evals.prompt: I'm going to launch 30 background Agent calls, one per file, each with intelligent-delegate:worker, and handle each result as it comes in. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: The tier is fine, the shape is not: 30 background completions are 30 orchestrator wake-ups, each re-reading the context. Thirty similar items is rule 5: a Workflow with pipeline(), agentType on every call, which returns one result.
expectations: It routes 30 similar items to a Workflow (pipeline) rather than 30 separate Agent calls
It names the orchestrator cost of 30 background completions: each one starts an orchestrator turn that re-reads the whole context
It keeps an agentType on every agent() call in the Workflow
It does not tell the user to switch the tier to the session model or to drop the tier

evals.prompt: My shell profile exports CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL=max. I pinned my review fan-out to intelligent-delegate:inspector, which is medium. So the reviewers run at medium, right?
evals.expected_output: No: CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL beats both a definition's effort and the call's effort, so every tier runs at max. Unset it (or set it to the level you want) for the session that spawns the agents.
expectations: It says the reviewers will NOT run at medium
It explains that CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL overrides both the definition's frontmatter effort and the call-site effort
It recommends unsetting or changing the environment variable for the session that spawns the agents

evals.prompt: I'm in an Opus session. To save money I'll send all my 'find where X is defined' searches across this huge repo to Explore, since it's the cheap built-in. Right?
evals.expected_output: Explore has the smallest cold-start prefix but runs on the session's model, so in an Opus session it is an Opus call. For a large locate whose answer you can check, scout (Haiku) is cheaper; for a read you will act on, inspector.
expectations: It says Explore runs on the session's model (Opus here), so it is not the cheap option in an Opus session
It acknowledges Explore's smaller prefix (no CLAUDE.md, no git status) as its only cost advantage
It recommends scout for a large locate whose answer can be checked, or inspector for a read the user will act on
